title: Projector Screen Size Chart: 100 and 120-Inch Dimensions
metaDescription: A 100-inch 16:9 screen is 87.2 x 49 inches; a 120-inch is 104.6 x 58.8 inches. Dimensions chart for 80 to 150-inch screens in 16:9, 2.35:1 and 4:3.
keywords: how big is a 100 inch screen
what size projector screen do i need
intro:
A **100-inch** 16:9 projector screen is **87.2 inches wide and 49.0 inches tall** (about 7 ft 3 in × 4 ft 1 in). A **120-inch** screen is **104.6 × 58.8 inches** (8 ft 9 in × 4 ft 11 in), and a 125-inch is 108.9 × 61.3 inches. Screen sizes are diagonals, so the width and height depend on the aspect ratio.

The chart below gives the viewable width, height and area for every common size, the seat distance THX's 40-degree guide suggests, and the same sizes in 2.35:1 and 4:3. Add the frame or case on top: it varies by model, so check the listing.
quickAnswer: **16:9 screen dimensions:** 100-inch = 87.2 × 49.0 in; 110-inch = 95.9 × 53.9 in; 120-inch = 104.6 × 58.8 in; 125-inch = 108.9 × 61.3 in; 135-inch = 117.7 × 66.2 in; 150-inch = 130.7 × 73.5 in. Width = diagonal × 0.872; height = diagonal × 0.490. These are viewable areas, so add the frame to get the wall space.

sections.heading: Projector screen size chart (16:9)
sections.body:
| Diagonal | Width | Height | Width × height (ft) | Screen area | THX seat distance |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 80-inch | 69.7 in | 39.2 in | 5 ft 10 in × 3 ft 3 in | 19.0 sq ft | 8 ft 0 in |
| 92-inch | 80.2 in | 45.1 in | 6 ft 8 in × 3 ft 9 in | 25.1 sq ft | 9 ft 2 in |
| 100-inch | 87.2 in | 49.0 in | 7 ft 3 in × 4 ft 1 in | 29.7 sq ft | 10 ft 0 in |
| 106-inch | 92.4 in | 52.0 in | 7 ft 8 in × 4 ft 4 in | 33.3 sq ft | 10 ft 7 in |
| 110-inch | 95.9 in | 53.9 in | 8 ft 0 in × 4 ft 6 in | 35.9 sq ft | 11 ft 0 in |
| 120-inch | 104.6 in | 58.8 in | 8 ft 9 in × 4 ft 11 in | 42.7 sq ft | 12 ft 0 in |
| 125-inch | 108.9 in | 61.3 in | 9 ft 1 in × 5 ft 1 in | 46.4 sq ft | 12 ft 6 in |
| 135-inch | 117.7 in | 66.2 in | 9 ft 10 in × 5 ft 6 in | 54.1 sq ft | 13 ft 6 in |
| 150-inch | 130.7 in | 73.5 in | 10 ft 11 in × 6 ft 2 in | 66.8 sq ft | 15 ft 0 in |

The last column is the distance from your eyes to the screen for the THX 40-degree view. For the full range of seat distances, see the [TV and screen viewing distance chart](/tv-size-viewing-distance-chart/).

sections.heading: How big is a 100-inch screen?
sections.body: A 100-inch 16:9 screen is **87.2 inches wide by 49.0 inches tall** (7 ft 3 in × 4 ft 1 in), about 29.7 square feet of picture. On a standard 8-foot (96-inch) wall it leaves about 47 inches of height, so mount the bottom edge 24 to 36 inches off the floor depending on seating. A budget pull-down like the [Elite Screens Manual B](/gear/elite-screens-manual-b/) ($80–$150) comes in this size.

sections.heading: How big is a 120-inch screen?
sections.body: A 120-inch 16:9 screen is **104.6 inches wide by 58.8 inches tall** (8 ft 9 in × 4 ft 11 in), about 42.7 square feet. You need a wall at least 9 feet wide once the frame is added. THX's 40-degree guide puts the main seat about 12 feet away. Fixed-frame options in this size include the [Silver Ticket STR-169120](/gear/silver-ticket-str-169120/) and [Elite Screens Sable Frame 2](/gear/elite-screens-sable-frame-2/). A 125-inch screen adds about 4 inches of width and 2.5 inches of height.

sections.heading: Screen dimensions in 16:9, 2.35:1 and 4:3
sections.body:
| Diagonal | 16:9 (W × H) | 2.35:1 (W × H) | 4:3 (W × H) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100-inch | 87.2 × 49.0 in | 92.0 × 39.2 in | 80.0 × 60.0 in |
| 120-inch | 104.6 × 58.8 in | 110.4 × 47.0 in | 96.0 × 72.0 in |
| 125-inch | 108.9 × 61.3 in | 115.0 × 48.9 in | 100.0 × 75.0 in |
| 135-inch | 117.7 × 66.2 in | 124.2 × 52.9 in | 108.0 × 81.0 in |
| 150-inch | 130.7 × 73.5 in | 138.0 × 58.7 in | 120.0 × 90.0 in |

The same diagonal gives a wider, shorter picture in 2.35:1 (CinemaScope) and a narrower, taller one in 4:3. For films shot in scope, a 2.35:1 screen avoids black bars, but 16:9 TV and streaming content then shows bars on the sides. Most home theaters use 16:9.

sections.heading: What size projector screen do I need?
sections.body:
Work through three limits and take the smallest:

1. **Wall width:** screen width plus frame, with some space either side for speakers.
2. **Seat distance:** divide your seat distance in inches by about 1.2 for the THX view. At 11 feet (132 inches), that is about 110 inches.
3. **Projector distance:** your projector's throw ratio and mount position cap the size. Check the [projector throw distance chart](/projector-throw-distance-chart/).

Brightness is the fourth check: the same light spread over 42.7 square feet (120-inch) instead of 29.7 (100-inch) is about 30% dimmer per square foot, so in rooms with some light, a smaller screen or brighter projector helps.

sections.heading: Does screen gain or material change the size you should pick?
sections.body: Gain changes how bright the image looks, not its size. A gain of about 1.1, common on the white screens we track, reflects slightly more light toward the seats than a matte white wall. Grey and [ALR screens](/glossary/alr-screen/) like the [Elite Screens CineGrey 3D](/gear/elite-screens-cinegrey-3d/) (gain 1.2) help in rooms with ambient light. See the [best projector screen for home theater](/best-projector-screen-for-home-theater/).

mistakes.title: Forgetting the frame
mistakes.body: Listed sizes are the viewable picture. Fixed frames add a border on every side, so measure the full outer dimensions from the listing.

mistakes.title: Picking a size before placing the projector
mistakes.body: If the projector cannot sit far enough back, it will not fill the screen. Check the throw distance first.

mistakes.title: Going too big for the room light
mistakes.body: A larger screen spreads the same lumens thinner. In a room with daylight, size down or add an ALR screen.

mistakes.title: Mounting the screen too high
mistakes.body: Keep the centre of the picture near seated eye height for the front row, unless a second row needs the bottom edge raised.

faqs.q: What are the dimensions of a 100-inch projector screen?
faqs.a: A 100-inch 16:9 screen is 87.2 inches wide and 49.0 inches tall, about 7 ft 3 in by 4 ft 1 in. In 4:3 it is 80 by 60 inches.

faqs.q: What are the dimensions of a 120-inch screen?
faqs.a: A 120-inch 16:9 screen is 104.6 inches wide and 58.8 inches tall, about 8 ft 9 in by 4 ft 11 in. In 2.35:1 it is 110.4 by 47.0 inches.
108.9 inches wide and 61.3 inches tall in 16:9, about 9 ft 1 in by 5 ft 1 in, before the frame.

faqs.q: How far should I sit from a 120-inch screen?
faqs.a: About 12 feet for the THX 40-degree view, and no more than about 16 feet for the SMPTE 30-degree minimum.

faqs.q: Is 100 or 120 inches better for a home theater?
faqs.a: 120 inches suits rooms where you sit 11 to 14 feet away and can control light. 100 inches fits seats around 10 feet away, smaller walls and rooms with some ambient light.

faqs.q: How do I calculate screen dimensions from the diagonal?
faqs.a: For 16:9, width = diagonal × 0.8716 and height = diagonal × 0.4903. For 4:3, width = diagonal × 0.8 and height = diagonal × 0.6.

bottomLine: A 100-inch 16:9 screen is **87.2 × 49.0 inches** and a 120-inch is **104.6 × 58.8 inches**, before the frame. Pick the size your wall, seats and projector all allow: the [viewing distance chart](/tv-size-viewing-distance-chart/) covers seats and the [throw distance chart](/projector-throw-distance-chart/) covers the projector. Then choose a screen from the [best projector screen for home theater](/best-projector-screen-for-home-theater/).
